cards.title: CI/CD for ML — How It Differs from CI/CD for Code
cards.teaser: Software CI/CD validates behavior against static test cases. ML CI/CD must also validate data, model weights, statistical properties, and fairness metrics — none of which are deterministic artifacts. The pipeline gets a new dimension: the training pipeline itself is a build step.

runs.text: In conventional software CI/CD the artifact under test is deterministic: the same source code, built with the same compiler, produces the same binary. Tests assert fixed expectations. A test that passed yesterday passes today unless code changed.
ML CI/CD inherits all of that and adds three new concerns:

items.text: Training the same model twice on the same data rarely produces identical weights. Tests must tolerate statistical variation while still catching meaningful regressions.
Code correctness is not sufficient — data correctness must also be verified. A model trained on schema-violating or stale data can pass all code tests and still be worthless.
The "compile" equivalent in ML is the training run. The pipeline must orchestrate data validation, training, evaluation, fairness testing, and packaging before any deployment can happen.

runs.text: This produces a pipeline with at least two parallel tracks. The
code track
validates transforms, feature logic, and serving code — just like conventional CI. The
model track
validates data, trains the model, runs behavioral and fairness evaluations, and packages the model artifact for deployment.

The seminal framing comes from Sculley et al., "Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems" (NeurIPS, 2015), which argued that ML systems accrue technical debt much faster than software systems because there are more moving parts that can silently degrade — data, features, models, and code.

Normal CI checks whether your code is correct. ML CI also has to check whether your data is correct and whether your model behaves correctly — and the model itself is a non-deterministic artifact that gets rebuilt (retrained) as part of the pipeline.

cards.title: Testing Data — Schema Validation, Distribution Checks, Freshness
cards.teaser: Data tests are the foundation of ML CI. Before training, the pipeline must verify that input data has the expected schema, that feature distributions have not silently shifted, and that the data is fresh enough to be meaningful.

runs.text: A model trained on bad data will produce bad predictions — and bad data rarely triggers an exception. Without explicit data tests, data quality failures are silent.
The three categories of data tests that belong in every ML CI pipeline:

items.text: Assert that the dataset has the expected columns, types, and cardinalities. Tools: Great Expectations, TFX Data Validation (TFDV), Pandera. Example: assert that
is in {0, 1}, and that no required column has more than 1% nulls.

Compare the current batch's feature distributions against a reference baseline (typically the training distribution). Use statistical tests: KS-test for continuous features, chi-squared for categoricals. Flag features whose drift score exceeds a threshold — not necessarily fail, but surface for human review.

Assert that the data was generated within an acceptable window. A nightly training job fed last week's data because an upstream ETL silently failed is a common silent failure mode. A freshness check gates the pipeline before training begins.

runs.text: TensorFlow Extended (TFX) ships a
ExampleValidator

component that runs schema and anomaly checks as a pipeline step, emitting a validation artifact consumed by downstream components. Great Expectations provides equivalent functionality and integrates with Airflow, dbt, and Spark pipelines.
Data tests must run on the actual training batch, not on a sample from a previous run. Caching data validation results from last week defeats the purpose entirely.

Before training, check three things about your data: does it have the right shape and types (schema), are the distributions close to what they were before (distribution), and was it generated recently enough to still be useful (freshness)? If any of these fail, stop the pipeline — garbage in, garbage out.

cards.title: Testing Models — Behavior Tests, Invariance Tests, Directional Tests
cards.teaser: The CheckList paper (Ribeiro et al., ACL 2020) gave ML practitioners a rigorous framework for model behavioral testing — three test types that catch failure modes invisible to aggregate accuracy metrics.

runs.text: Aggregate metrics like accuracy or AUC summarize model performance across a dataset. They are necessary but not sufficient: a model can have high accuracy while systematically failing on specific subpopulations, specific phrasings, or specific input perturbations.
Marco Tulio Ribeiro et al. introduced
CheckList
at ACL 2020 ("Beyond Accuracy: Behavioral Testing of NLP Models with CheckList") as a structured approach to behavioral testing. The three test types generalize beyond NLP to any predictive model:

items.text: Test that the model handles basic cases it should clearly get right. For a sentiment classifier: "This product is great" → positive, "This product is terrible" → negative. These are regression tests — if the model fails them after retraining, something has gone wrong.

Perturb the input in ways that should not change the prediction. For a loan risk model: changing the applicant's name from "James" to "Jamal" should not change the predicted risk score. Invariance tests expose spurious correlations and fairness failures.

Perturb the input in ways that should change the prediction in a known direction. For a house price model: adding a bedroom to an identical house should increase (not decrease) the predicted price. Direction violations indicate the model has learned the wrong relationship.

runs.text: In CI, these tests run against a fixed evaluation dataset generated offline. Each test category produces a pass/fail result that gates promotion to the model registry. A model that fails invariance tests — even with high overall accuracy — should not be deployed.

CheckList is available as an open-source library (github.com/marcotcr/checklist). It includes a template-based perturbation generator that makes writing large suites of behavioral tests practical. The paper won the ACL 2020 Best Paper award.

After training, run three behavioral checks on the model: does it get the obvious cases right (MFT), does it stay consistent when you change irrelevant details (invariance), and does it change in the right direction when you change relevant details (directional)? High accuracy alone doesn't tell you any of these things.

cards.title: Fairness Tests — Disaggregated Metrics, Demographic Parity, Equal Opportunity
cards.teaser: A model that performs well on average can perform badly for specific demographic groups. Fairness tests measure disaggregated performance across protected attributes and enforce quantitative constraints before any model reaches production.

runs.text: Aggregate metrics hide subgroup performance. A hiring model with 90% accuracy might have 95% accuracy for one demographic group and 70% for another. Without disaggregated evaluation, this disparity is invisible until it causes harm.
The three most widely used fairness metrics in CI gates:

items.text: Compute accuracy, precision, recall, and AUC separately for each demographic subgroup (gender, race, age bracket). Assert that no group falls below a minimum threshold and that the gap between the best and worst performing groups is below a maximum tolerance.

The positive prediction rate should be equal (within tolerance) across groups: P(Ŷ=1 | A=0) ≈ P(Ŷ=1 | A=1). Example: if a loan model approves 60% of applications from group A, it should approve approximately 60% from group B. This is a weaker criterion that does not account for base rate differences.

The true positive rate (recall) should be equal across groups: P(Ŷ=1 | Y=1, A=0) ≈ P(Ŷ=1 | Y=1, A=1). This is the Hardt et al. criterion ("Equality of Opportunity in Supervised Learning", NeurIPS 2016): among qualified applicants, all groups should be approved at the same rate.

runs.text: In CI, fairness tests are implemented as assertions on a held-out evaluation dataset that includes protected attribute labels. Google's
Fairness Indicators
library and IBM's
AI Fairness 360
both produce reports suitable for pipeline gating. A model that violates fairness thresholds is blocked from promotion regardless of its aggregate performance.

Fairness metrics are mutually incompatible in general: demographic parity, equal opportunity, and calibration cannot all be satisfied simultaneously when base rates differ across groups (Chouldechova, 2017). Choose the criterion appropriate to the use case before writing the pipeline gate.

Fairness tests slice the evaluation data by demographic group and check that the model treats each group equitably. Demographic parity checks whether prediction rates are equal; equal opportunity checks whether the model catches qualified candidates at equal rates. Both become pipeline gates that block deployment when violated.

cards.title: The Training-Serving Skew Problem
cards.teaser: Training-serving skew is the bug class that arises when the code that prepares features for training is different from the code that prepares features at serving time — even when the intent is identical. It is the most insidious source of production model failures.

runs.text: Training-serving skew happens when the feature preprocessing applied during training diverges — even slightly — from the preprocessing applied at inference time. The model then receives inputs during serving that differ from what it was trained on, degrading prediction quality in ways that are almost impossible to debug from model metrics alone.
Common manifestations:

items.text: The training pipeline normalizes a feature as
using the training set's mean and standard deviation. The serving code copies this logic but uses hardcoded values from a different time period. When distributions shift, the two paths diverge.

Training runs in Python 3.9 with pandas 1.3; serving runs in Python 3.11 with pandas 2.1. Subtle behavioral differences in string encoding, float rounding, or NaN handling produce different feature values from identical raw inputs.
Training imputes nulls with the median; serving uses 0. The model was never trained on 0-imputed features.

runs.text: The canonical solution is to use
a single shared feature transformation library
that both the training pipeline and the serving stack import. TFX's
Transform

component serializes transformations as a TensorFlow graph embedded in the SavedModel, so the identical computation runs during both training and serving. Feature stores (Feast, Tecton) provide a similar guarantee via a unified feature retrieval API.
In CI, training-serving skew is caught by
distribution comparison tests

: after the model is trained, run the serving preprocessing code on the training dataset and compare the resulting features to those produced by the training preprocessing code. Any distributional difference is a skew signal.

Training-serving skew is particularly dangerous because it is silent. The model does not error — it just predicts on systematically different inputs than it was trained on. Without an explicit CI test comparing both preprocessing paths, it will reach production undetected.

Training-serving skew happens when the code that prepares data for training is even slightly different from the code that prepares data at prediction time. The model was trained on different inputs than it will receive in production, so it performs worse — and there is no error, just quietly wrong predictions. The fix is to share a single preprocessing path between both environments.

cards.title: Smoke Tests for Serving — Does the Deployed Model Load and Predict?
cards.teaser: A smoke test for a deployed model answers one minimal question: given a valid input, does the endpoint load, accept the request, and return a prediction in the expected format? It catches deployment failures that model evaluation cannot.

runs.text: Model evaluation tests whether a trained model is accurate. Smoke tests ask a prior question: is the model actually deployed and reachable? A model can pass all offline evaluations and still fail to serve because of a corrupt model artifact, a missing environment variable, a package version mismatch in the serving container, or a misconfigured routing rule.
A standard ML serving smoke test does three things:

items.text: probe and assert HTTP 200. This confirms the container started and the model loaded from storage.

Send a known valid input and assert that the response has the expected schema (correct field names, correct types), that prediction scores are in [0, 1] for classifiers, and that latency is below a maximum threshold.
Send a deliberately malformed request and assert the server returns a 400 with a useful error message rather than a 500 — confirming that input validation is in place.

runs.text: Smoke tests run in the CD pipeline
after
deployment to a staging environment and before any traffic is routed to the new version. A smoke test failure triggers an automatic rollback before any user is affected.
TensorFlow Serving, Triton Inference Server, and BentoML all expose standard health and readiness probes. Make smoke tests part of the CD pipeline's post-deploy step, not a separate manual checklist.

A smoke test asks one question after deployment: "Can I actually call this model and get a prediction back?" It catches container failures, missing artifacts, and broken routing that offline model evaluation will never find. Run it automatically after every deployment, before any real traffic is sent.

cards.title: Performance Benchmarks — Latency and Throughput Regression Tests
cards.teaser: A model that is accurate but too slow is not deployable. Latency and throughput regression tests run in CI to ensure that a new model version does not degrade serving performance below contractual SLOs.

runs.text: Model retraining that improves accuracy can simultaneously increase model size, inference complexity, or memory footprint — degrading latency. Without automated benchmarks in CI, this tradeoff is invisible until the model reaches production and SLO violations appear.
The two performance properties to benchmark:

items.text: Measure the time from request to prediction under a realistic request pattern. Assert that p99 latency is below the SLO threshold (e.g., 200ms). Use percentiles, not averages — a model that is fast 95% of the time but hangs for 5 seconds 1% of the time has a serious tail latency problem.

Measure the maximum stable request rate the serving instance can sustain without latency degradation. Assert that throughput has not regressed by more than X% from the baseline. This catches changes that increase per-request resource consumption.

runs.text: Benchmark implementation pattern: maintain a fixed load test script (Locust, k6, or wrk) that runs a standardized request mix. Run it against the candidate model in a dedicated benchmark environment before promotion. Store the baseline in the model registry alongside the model artifact. Gate promotion if any SLO threshold is breached.
For large models, also benchmark
memory footprint
and
cold-start time
(the time from container start to first successful prediction). Both affect scaling behavior and Kubernetes pod restart budgets.

Run benchmarks on hardware that matches production. Benchmarking on a shared CI runner with variable CPU contention produces noisy results. Use a dedicated, fixed-spec benchmark environment or measure regression relative to a baseline run on the same runner in the same pipeline.

A more accurate model that responds too slowly is still a failed deployment. Performance benchmarks in CI measure latency and throughput against the previous version and block promotion if they regress. Run them in the pipeline before the model reaches staging — not after users start complaining.

cards.title: Automated Retraining Triggers — Schedule, Drift, Performance
cards.teaser: Continuous Training (CT) extends CI/CD into the temporal dimension: models are automatically retrained when time passes, data drifts, or production metrics degrade. Each trigger type has different tradeoffs in cost, latency, and sensitivity.

runs.text: Unlike software, a deployed model degrades passively even when no code changes. The world changes, the data distribution shifts, and the model becomes progressively less aligned with current reality. Automated retraining triggers ensure the model stays fresh without requiring manual intervention.
The three trigger categories:

items.text: Retrain on a fixed cadence: daily, weekly, or monthly. Simple to implement and reason about. The right choice when data arrives in regular batches and the domain changes slowly. Drawback: triggers unnecessary retraining when data has not changed, and may trigger too late when it has changed rapidly.

Retrain when input feature distributions or output label distributions drift beyond a threshold. Uses the same statistical tests as data monitoring (KS-test, PSI — Population Stability Index). More responsive than schedule-based but requires a reliable monitoring pipeline and threshold tuning to avoid excessive false positives.

Retrain when production model metrics (accuracy, AUC, precision, recall) degrade below an SLO threshold. The most directly business-relevant trigger, but requires labeled ground-truth data in production — which is often delayed by days or weeks (label latency). Use performance triggers in combination with drift triggers for fast initial detection.

runs.text: In practice, teams combine all three: schedule as a backstop, drift as an early warning, and performance as the definitive gate. The retraining pipeline is triggered via a webhook or event bus message and runs the same CI/CD pipeline as a code-triggered run.

Google's MLOps whitepaper ("Practitioners Guide to MLOps", 2021) distinguishes ML Maturity Level 1 (manual retraining) from Level 2 (automated retraining pipeline) from Level 3 (automated CT with CI/CD). Most organizations operate at Level 1; drift-triggered CT is a Level 2 practice.

Models go stale as the world changes. Automated retraining watches for three signals: time passing (schedule), data distributions shifting (drift), or actual predictions getting worse (performance degradation). When any of these fires, it kicks off the training pipeline automatically — no human required.

cards.title: Continuous Training Pipelines — Kubeflow, Airflow, Vertex AI
cards.teaser: A Continuous Training pipeline is a DAG that orchestrates data validation, training, evaluation, and model registration as a repeatable, automated workflow. Kubeflow Pipelines, Apache Airflow, and Vertex AI Pipelines are the three dominant runtimes.

runs.text: A CT pipeline is not a CI pipeline that happens to train a model — it is a managed workflow with its own artifact lineage, retry logic, and caching semantics. The outputs of each step (validated dataset, trained model, evaluation report, fairness report) are tracked as named artifacts in a metadata store.
A minimal Kubeflow Pipelines (KFP) pipeline definition, using the KFP v2 SDK:

explanation.code:
# pipeline.yaml (compiled from KFP Python SDK)
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Workflow
metadata:
  name: ml-training-pipeline
spec:
  entrypoint: pipeline
  templates:
    - name: pipeline
      dag:
        tasks:
          - name: validate-data
            template: validate-data-step
          - name: train-model
            dependencies: [validate-data]
            template: train-model-step
          - name: evaluate-model
            dependencies: [train-model]
            template: evaluate-model-step
          - name: register-model
            dependencies: [evaluate-model]
            template: register-model-step
    - name: validate-data-step
      container:
        image: my-registry/data-validator:v1.2
        command: [python, validate.py]
    - name: train-model-step
      container:
        image: my-registry/trainer:v3.1
        command: [python, train.py, --epochs, "50"]
    - name: evaluate-model-step
      container:
        image: my-registry/evaluator:v2.0
        command: [python, evaluate.py, --threshold, "0.85"]
    - name: register-model-step
      container:
        image: my-registry/registry-client:v1.0
        command: [python, register.py]

runs.text: The three runtimes compared:

items.text: Kubernetes-native. Pipelines are compiled to Argo Workflows. Each step runs in its own container. Built-in artifact tracking via ML Metadata (MLMD). Best for: teams already running Kubernetes who want tight infrastructure control.

General-purpose workflow orchestrator widely adopted for data pipelines. Supports ML workflows via KubernetesPodOperator. Less ML-native than KFP — no built-in model artifact tracking, but highly extensible. Best for: organizations with existing Airflow infrastructure.
Managed KFP on Google Cloud. No infrastructure to manage. Pre-built components for BigQuery, AutoML, and model registry integration. Best for: GCP shops that want a managed, serverless CT pipeline.

runs.text: A Continuous Training pipeline is a reproducible workflow that runs the full training process — validate data, train, evaluate, register — automatically and on demand. Kubeflow runs it on Kubernetes, Airflow is a more general orchestrator, and Vertex AI is the fully managed GCP version. All three produce a lineage of artifacts you can audit and reproduce.

cards.title: CD for Models — Gradual Rollout, Blue/Green, Canary
cards.teaser: Model deployment requires the same gradual rollout patterns as software deployment — but the failure signal is statistical, not binary. A bad model does not return HTTP 500; it returns predictions that are subtly wrong. The rollout strategy must account for this.

runs.text: Serving infrastructure patterns (blue/green, canary) apply directly to model deployment, but with one critical difference: model failures are often statistical rather than structural. A broken microservice returns a 500 error. A degraded model returns a valid prediction that happens to be wrong more often. Traffic-splitting strategies must therefore be paired with metrics-based rollback triggers.

items.text: Run the current model (blue) and the new model (green) as separate endpoints behind a load balancer. Switch 100% of traffic to green at a designated cutover point. If green fails smoke tests or early metrics, switch back to blue instantly. Zero-downtime, zero-risk transition with full rollback capability.

Route a small percentage of real traffic (e.g., 5%) to the new model while the remainder goes to the current model. Monitor prediction quality, latency, and business metrics on the canary slice. Gradually increase the canary percentage — 5% → 25% → 50% → 100% — if metrics stay healthy. Any metric regression at any step triggers automatic rollback.

Send requests to both models but serve only the current model's predictions to users. Log both predictions and compare offline. Shadow mode is invaluable for validating behavioral parity between model versions before exposing the new model to live traffic.

runs.text: Kubernetes-native serving stacks (KServe, Seldon Core) support all three patterns via traffic splitting annotations. AWS SageMaker and Vertex AI Model Registry support canary and blue/green natively. The key instrumentation requirement: each prediction must be tagged with its model version so metrics can be disaggregated per deployment slice.
Shadow mode is particularly useful when the new model uses a different feature schema — you can validate that the new preprocessing path produces sensible outputs before any user depends on them.

Don't flip all traffic to a new model at once. Blue/green keeps the old model ready to switch back instantly. Canary gradually moves traffic while you watch the metrics. Shadow mode runs the new model in parallel without using its predictions — just to see how it would behave. All three require tagging each prediction with its model version so you can measure the new model's quality separately.

cards.title: Rollback Patterns for Models — Keep the Previous Version Warm
cards.teaser: Rolling back a model is not the same as rolling back code. The previous model version must be kept in a warm state — loaded, healthy, and immediately servable — so that rollback is a traffic switch, not a redeploy.

runs.text: In software deployment, rollback means reverting a container image and restarting a pod — a process that takes seconds on modern orchestrators. In model deployment, a naive rollback means re-downloading the previous model artifact from storage, loading it into memory, and restarting the serving process. For large models, this can take minutes — long enough to cause an SLO breach.
The solution is to keep the previous model version in a warm serving state throughout the canary or rollout window:

items.text: The blue/green pattern inherently provides a warm previous version — the blue endpoint remains loaded and healthy until the green deployment is declared stable and the blue endpoint is explicitly decommissioned. Rollback is a load balancer rule change: zero latency.

The model registry (MLflow, Vertex AI Model Registry, SageMaker Model Registry) maintains every version with a lifecycle state: Staging, Production, Archived. Rollback is a state transition: demote the current Production version to Archived, promote the previous version back to Production.

Define a rollback condition in the CD pipeline: if the canary slice's metrics (prediction error rate, latency p99, business KPI) degrade beyond a threshold within the observation window, trigger rollback automatically. Platforms like Argo Rollouts and Flagger implement this pattern with configurable analysis templates.

runs.text: One important operational constraint:
model versioning must be coupled with serving schema versioning.

If the new model version was trained on a different feature schema than the old model, rolling back the model without rolling back the feature preprocessing code creates a new instance of the training-serving skew problem.

Never decommission the previous model version immediately after a rollout. Maintain at least the previous two model versions in a servable state until the new version has been stable in production for the full observation window (typically 24–72 hours).

Rolling back a model should be as fast as flipping a switch, not as slow as reloading a large file from disk. Keep the previous version loaded and ready. If the new version's metrics go bad, the rollback is a traffic rule change — instant. Only retire the previous version once the new one has been stable long enough to trust.

cards.title: Model CI Workflows — GitHub Actions and GitLab CI Patterns
cards.teaser: Training on PR is the ML equivalent of running tests on PR: every proposed change to training code, feature logic, or model configuration triggers a lightweight training run whose output is evaluated and posted back to the pull request.

runs.text: Training on pull request (also called train-on-PR or model-CI) closes the feedback loop between code change and model behavior. Without it, a change to a feature transformer might silently degrade model quality — and this will only be discovered the next time someone runs a manual training job.
A minimal GitHub Actions model-CI workflow:

explanation.code:
# .github/workflows/model-ci.yml
name: Model CI
on:
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - 'src/features/**'
      - 'src/training/**'
      - 'configs/model_config.yaml'

jobs:
  model-ci:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Validate training data schema
        run: python scripts/validate_data.py --dataset data/train_sample.parquet

      - name: Train model on sample dataset
        run: |
          python src/training/train.py \
            --config configs/model_config.yaml \
            --dataset data/train_sample.parquet \
            --output artifacts/candidate_model

      - name: Run behavioral tests (CheckList)
        run: python scripts/run_checklist.py --model artifacts/candidate_model

      - name: Run fairness tests
        run: python scripts/run_fairness.py --model artifacts/candidate_model

      - name: Compare against baseline
        run: |
          python scripts/compare_models.py \
            --candidate artifacts/candidate_model \
            --baseline models/production_baseline \
            --output artifacts/comparison_report.json

      - name: Post results to PR
        uses: actions/github-script@v7
        with:
          script: |
            const fs = require('fs');
            const report = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync('artifacts/comparison_report.json'));
            github.rest.issues.createComment({
              issue_number: context.issue.number,
              owner: context.repo.owner,
              repo: context.repo.repo,
              body: `## Model CI Results\n\n${report.summary}`
            });

runs.text: Two key design decisions:
path filters
ensure the expensive training step only runs when ML-relevant files change (not on documentation edits), and
sample datasets
keep the PR training job fast (minutes, not hours). The PR training run is a canary signal, not a production training run.

Model CI means: every time someone proposes a change to the training code or feature logic, the pipeline automatically trains a model on a small dataset, runs the behavioral and fairness tests, compares it to the current production model, and posts the results to the pull request. Engineers can see whether their code change helped or hurt the model before merging.

cards.title: The Test Pyramid for ML
cards.teaser: The software test pyramid — many unit tests, fewer integration tests, fewest E2E tests — has a direct ML analog that maps test granularity to the four layers of an ML system: transforms, pipelines, models, and live endpoints.

runs.text: Mike Cohn's test pyramid principle — fast, cheap tests at the bottom; slow, expensive tests at the top — applies to ML systems with a four-layer structure. Each layer has distinct test characteristics, failure modes, and placement in the CI/CD pipeline.

items.text: Layer 1 — Unit tests on transforms (base of pyramid).

Test individual feature transformation functions in isolation: does the normalization function handle nulls correctly, does the tokenizer produce the expected output for edge-case strings, does the one-hot encoder handle unseen categories gracefully? These tests run in milliseconds, require no data infrastructure, and belong in the standard CI pipeline.

Test that the full data preprocessing pipeline runs end-to-end on a small sample dataset, produces the expected artifact schema, and is consistent between the training and serving paths (training-serving skew tests). These tests take minutes and run on every PR that touches ML code.

The CheckList MFT, INV, and DIR tests described in card 3, plus fairness tests and performance benchmarks. These tests require a trained model artifact and take longer — they run on the model produced by the CT pipeline before promotion to the model registry.
Layer 4 — E2E tests on deployed predictions (apex of pyramid).

Smoke tests, live canary monitoring, and production metric tracking. These tests run against the actual deployed endpoint with real or realistic traffic. The slowest and most expensive layer — run them last, after the model has passed all lower layers.

runs.text: The pyramid shape matters: if you skip layers 1 and 2 and rely entirely on layer 3 and 4 tests, failures surface too late and are too expensive to fix. A bug in a feature transform that is caught by a layer-1 unit test costs minutes to fix; the same bug caught by a layer-4 E2E test in production costs hours or days.

The ML test pyramid is formalized in Google's testing taxonomy for ML systems (Breck et al., "The ML Test Score", IEEE BigData 2017), which proposes 28 specific tests across four categories: data, model, infrastructure, and monitoring. The paper provides a scoring rubric for assessing ML system test maturity.

The ML test pyramid has four layers from bottom to top: unit tests on individual transform functions (fast, many), integration tests on the full preprocessing pipeline (medium), behavioral and fairness tests on the trained model (slow, few), and E2E smoke tests on the live endpoint (slowest, fewest). Don't skip the bottom layers — bugs caught at layer 1 are 100x cheaper to fix than bugs caught at layer 4.
